subject: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item

messages.author: 9ec69ca07f36d6a1
messages.subject: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
I have an application where I developed 4 LaTeX sections to do various analyses on a set of variables.  There is one principal independent variable.  Now I want to create 4 sections for each of three other primary independent variables.  What is a good way to reuse code and sentences to minimize typing for the last 3 sections?  I see how to reuse chunks if code doesn't change at all, but I don't see how to reuse chunks with variable substitution or how to reuse LaTeX sections and their associated chunks.

Secondly, would it be possible and a good idea to add a macro facility to knitr?  For example:

<<main, x=age>>=
lm(y ~ (*x*) + sex + height)
summary((*x*))
@

<<main,x=weight>>=
@

Thanks
Frank

messages.author: 9ec69ca07f36d6a1
messages.subject: Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
p.s.  I just did a test using the m4 macro preprocessor and it appears to be ideal for this task, allowing expansion of LaTeX text mixed with code chunks.  Arguments are referred to using $1 $2 etc.  An example:

define(var1, AaAa)
define(var2, BbBb)
This is an example of a variable var1 that refers to var2.
<<>>=
if(1==1){var2}
if(1==1){var2;var1}
if(1==1){var2,~var1}
@

define(`foreach',`ifelse(eval($#>2),1,
    `pushdef(`$1',`$3')$2`'popdef(`$1')dnl
  `'ifelse(eval($#>3),1,`$0(`$1',`$2',shift(shift(shift($@))))')')')
  
foreach(`X',`Open the X. ',`door',`window')

% See http://www.gnu.org/software/m4/manual/m4.html#Macros
define(`upcase',   `translit(`$*', `a-z', `A-Z')')
define(`downcase', `translit(`$*', `A-Z', `a-z')')
define(`_capitalize',
       `regexp(`$1', `^\(\w\)\(\w*\)',
       `upcase(`\1')`'downcase(`\2')')')
define(`capitalize', `patsubst(`$1', `\w+', `_$0(`\&')')')
     

define(`dothis', `
This is a multi-step analysis of $1.
This is the second line $2 upcase($2) / capitalize($2).
<<>>=
x <- $3
y@z
y$z
@
')

dothis(Aa, Bb, y.1)
dothis(Aaaa, kind of a hint, y.2_3_)

OUTPUT:

*m4 test.txt


This is an example of a variable AaAa that refers to BbBb.
<<>>=
if(1==1){BbBb}
if(1==1){BbBb;AaAa}
if(1==1){BbBb,~AaAa}
@


  
Open the door.   Open the window.   

% See http://www.gnu.org/software/m4/manual/m4.html#Macros




     




This is a multi-step analysis of Aa.
This is the second line Bb BB / Bb.
<<>>=
x <- y.1
y@z
y$z
@


This is a multi-step analysis of Aaaa.
This is the second line kind of a hint KIND OF A HINT / Kind Of A Hint.
<<>>=
x <- y.2_3_
y@z
y$z
@


Frank

messages.author: 9ec69ca07f36d6a1
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
Thanks for your notes Baptiste and Yihui.  I think that the syntax of pyexpander is cleaner for this purpose, and that Yihui's solution applies more to manipulating code chunks that it applies to mixtures of LaTeX sections and code chunks.  Pyexpander also allows full use of python code, and its string manipulation functions allow you to easily manipulate variable names, e.g. capitalizing the first word or appending a number to the end of the name.  The the R code that is emitted and that pretty prints with knitr has variable names nicely substituted.  The downside is that you have to escape R and LaTeX $ with \$.  Here's an example:

*cat ~/bin/pye2r 
# Example: pye2r test 'x="age.2";y="chol_3."' test2 (test.pye -> test2.Rnw)
expander.py --eval $2 $1.pye > $3.Rnw

*cat maker 
pye2r repbmd 'v="hip";oth1="lumbar";oth2="femur";oth3="forearm"' hip
pye2r repbmd 'v="lumbar";oth1="hip";oth2="femur";oth3="forearm"' lumbar
pye2r repbmd 'v="femur";oth1="hip";oth2="lumbar";oth3="forearm"' femur
pye2r repbmd 'v="forearm";oth1="hip";oth2="lumbar";oth3="femur"' forearm
cat hip.Rnw lumbar.Rnw femur.Rnw forearm.Rnw > allbmd.Rnw

*cat repbmd.pye
$begin
$extend(v,oth1,oth2,oth3)    $# allow referencing by $v not just $(v)
$py(v0=v+"0")                $# create new variable with 0 appended
$py(v26=v+"26")
$py(v52=v+"52")
$py(oth10=oth1+"0")
$py(oth20=oth2+"0")
$py(oth30=oth3+"0")
$py(vupper=str.title(v))     $# capitalize first letters
$extend(oth10,oth20,oth30,v0,v26,v52,vupper)  $# allow easy referencing of new var


\section{Analysis of $vupper Bone Mineral Density}
\subsection{26w Using Baseline Data}
In this section I model 26w interpolated BMD using baseline BMD (all
four measures, not just the target measure), baseline weight, age,
sex, race, \$t\$-score stratum, and treatment.  I first fit a saturated
model with respect to all of the continuous predictors, using
restricted cubic splines with 5 knots, then potentially use partial
\$\chi^2\$ (blinded to nonlinearity components) to reassign degrees
of freedom.  
<<results="tex">>=
f <- ols($v26 ~ sex*rcs($v0,5) + rcs($oth10,5) + rcs($oth20,5) +
         rcs($oth30,5) + sex*rcs(wt0,5) + trtp + rcs(age,5) + race + sex +
         blppar + bltscgrp, data=d)
print(f, coefs=FALSE, latex=TRUE)
lan(f)
@
...
$end

Resulting allbmd.Rnw:
\section{Analysis of Hip Bone Mineral Density}
\subsection{26w Using Baseline Data}
In this section I model 26w interpolated BMD using baseline BMD (all
four measures, not just the target measure), baseline weight, age,
sex, race, $t$-score stratum, and treatment.  I first fit a saturated
model with respect to all of the continuous predictors, using
restricted cubic splines with 5 knots, then potentially use partial
$\chi^2$ (blinded to nonlinearity components) to reassign degrees
of freedom.  
<<results="tex">>=
f <- ols(hip26 ~ sex*rcs(hip0,5) + rcs(lumbar0,5) + rcs(femur0,5) +
         rcs(forearm0,5) + sex*rcs(wt0,5) + trtp + rcs(age,5) + race + sex +
         blppar + bltscgrp, data=d)
print(f, coefs=FALSE, latex=TRUE)
lan(f)
@

The global test for nonlinearity is nowhere close to being significant, so
all nonlinear effects will be dropped.
...

Frank

I still don't see the benefits over preprocessing in R, e.g.

a = 5 # some variable
brew(text = 'Let this be a <%=a%>-th knitr chunk worth $$s,
<< <%= toupper(paste0("chunk-", a)) %>, results = "asis" >>=
plot(1, rnorm(<%= a %>))
title("freedom for $")
@')

then again, I haven't had to use either solution; in practice things
might be different, I would still be curious to hear what limitations
you find in the above.

baptiste

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
Hi Frank,

I just wrote a simple 'expander' in knitr as knit_expand() (currently
on Github), which should achieve the same goal as pyexpander in your
case; see https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/075-knit-expand.Rnw
for one example.

Your template would be like this:

-----------

{{
v0=paste0(v,"0") # create new variable with 0 appended
v26=paste0(v,"26")
v52=paste0(v,"52")
oth10=paste0(oth1,"0")
oth20=paste0(oth2,"0")
oth30=paste0(oth3,"0")
vupper=Hmisc::capitalize(v) # capitalize first letters
}}

\section{Analysis of {{vupper}} Bone Mineral Density}
\subsection{26w BMD and Baseline Predictors}

In this section I model 26w interpolated BMD using baseline BMD (all
four measures, not just the target measure), baseline weight, age,
sex, race, $t$-score stratum, and treatment. I first fit a saturated
model with respect to all of the continuous predictors, using
restricted cubic splines with 5 knots, then potentially use partial
$\chi^2$ (blinded to nonlinearity components) to reassign degrees
of freedom.

<<{{v}}-sat26,results="asis">>=
f <- ols({{v26}} ~ sex*rcs({{v0}},5) + rcs({{oth10}},5) + rcs({{oth20}},5) +
rcs({{oth30}},5) + sex*rcs(wt0,5) + trtp + rcs(age,5) + race + sex +

blppar + bltscgrp, data=d)
print(f, coefs=FALSE, latex=TRUE)
lan(f)
@

The global test for nonlinearity is nowhere close to being significant, so
all nonlinear effects will be dropped.

-----------

and you can expand the template by:

knit_expand("repbmd.pye", v="hip", oth1="lumbar", oth2="femur", oth3="forearm")

Actually you can vectorize the whole job by mapply():

mapply(knit_expand, file="repbmd.pye", v=c("hip", "lumbar", "femur",
"forearm"), oth1=c("lumbar", "hip", "hip", "hip"), oth2=c("femur",
"femur", "lumbar", "lumbar"), oth3=c("forearm", "forearm", "forearm",
"femur"))

This gives you the Rnw source, which is ready to be passed to knit().

I used {{}} as the tag instead of $() to avoid the awkward LaTeX math
delimiter problem, so you do not need to escape $.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
Perhaps the conditional generation can be achieved in pure R:

{{
if (v!="hip" && previous.result==3) "

.... LaTeX stuff ....
<<>>=
any number of code chunks
@
... more LaTeX text ...
"
}}

i.e. quote the text and they will appear when the condition is TRUE.

tpl = 'an analysis
{{
if (v!="hip" && previous.result==3) "
some text
<<>>=
rnorm(5)
@
more text
"
}}
conclusions'

previous.result=1
knit_expand(text = tpl, v='hip')

previous.result=3
knit_expand(text = tpl, v='hi')

If you feel the "" syntax is awkward, you can put that part in a file,
and use `{{ if (...) readLines('template.txt') }}` instead.

Regards,
Yihui

parts:
I guess the triple quote is not really necessary; at the moment I'm
thinking of removing the restriction on the code in {{}} so that we
can write incomplete expressions there, e.g.

{{ if (TRUE) { }}
text for true
{{ } else { }}
text for false
{{ } }}

{{ for (i in 1:10) { }}
text
{{ } }}

Actually this is just re-inventing the wheel of brew, but I think the
implementation will be cleaner.

In theory this will also affect the capability of \Sexpr{} and inline
R expressions in other document formats, e.g.

`r if (TRUE) {`
text
`r }`

But due to the poor choice of the delimiter \Sexpr{}, its curly braces
will restrict its power; "\Sexpr{ if (TRUE) { } text \Sexpr{ } }" will
not work.

Regards,

messages.author: c6ca7877bef91eef
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
parts:
R has had dedicated templating libraries like brew and whisker. Brew, in particular allows one to harness the full capabilities of R while working on repetitive documentation. Here is a solution that combines brew and knitr to generate reproducible reports with repetitive content. The basic idea is as follows.

1. Create a template for the document (use Rnwe as extension)
2. Preprocess the template using brew to generate Rnw
3. Knit the Rnw file to generate the final report.

Steps (2) and (3) can be combined into a single function as shown below.

brew_knit <- function(template, ...){
  input = gsub(".Rnwe", ".Rnw", template)
  brew(template, input)
  knit(input, ...)
}

Here is a gist that shows the Rnwe template and the resulting Rnw file.

https://gist.github.com/4565745 

Brew is very simple to use and has some very clever features that allow meta templates as well. Here is a great blog post that illustrates the power of brew

http://learnr.wordpress.com/2009/09/09/brew-creating-repetitive-reports/
